  keyboard shortcuts.
  11. Most multiplexers use a customizable prefix key sequence to intercept user commands.
  12. Scrollback buffers allow users to navigate and search through historical terminal
  output.
  13. Built-in copy modes let users select and copy text directly without touching a mouse.
  14. Configuration files allow comprehensive customization of keybindings, themes, and
  default layouts.
  15. Status bars display helpful system information like time, hostname, and active
  window titles.
  16. Multiple users can attach to the same session simultaneously to collaborate and pair
  program.
  17. Shell scripts can programmatically spawn predefined workspace layouts upon startup.
  18. Plugins and extensions can add capabilities such as battery meters, git status, and
  session managers.
  19. Session saving tools can restore open windows and directories across system reboots.
  20. Terminal multiplexers run with minimal overhead on low-resource remote servers.
  21. They provide terminal emulator independence by managing standard pseudo-terminals
  under the hood.
  22. GNU Screen was one of the earliest widespread terminal multiplexers created in 1987.
  23. tmux was developed as a modern, modular alternative to GNU Screen with a clean
  codebase.
  24. Zellij is a newer multiplexer written in Rust featuring built-in WebAssembly plugin
  support.
  25. Multiplexers protect long-running build or deployment jobs against unexpected
  terminal closures.
  26. Synchronized pane modes allow typing the same shell command across multiple hosts at
  once.
  27. Custom layouts can automatically arrange monitors, logs, and editor panes for
  development work.
  28. Nested multiplexer sessions can be controlled cleanly by using distinct prefix key
  bindings.
  29. Mouse support can optionally be toggled on for scrolling and clicking between active
  panes.
  30. Mastering a terminal multiplexer significantly boosts productivity in command-line
  environments.
